1:
Gill marks the seam: the laws of the preceding chapter seem finished, and what follows concerns vows, which a man was not obliged to make but made of his own freewill. Ellicott says the opening formula shows a separate divine communication, and that since the book alludes to vows repeatedly, a code designed above all to uphold the holiness of the sanctuary would be incomplete without defining the obligation of these self-imposed offerings. Henry turns it into a rule of piety: these are extraordinary vows, which God did not insist on, yet if consistent with the general precepts he would be well pleased with them, so that we should ask not only what we must do but what we may do for the glory of God, since as the liberal devises liberal things so the pious devises pious things.

Calvin distinguishes two ancient modes of consecration, the ban and the ordinary devoting for the use of the temple: the first might be laid on unclean animals and other unholy things, as on a whole city, but a vow properly could be made only of a clean man or animal. Wesley calls it an eminent or hard vow, not of things, which was customary, but of persons. Keil corrects the verb, that it means not to dedicate a vow but to make a special one. Ellicott reports the reading that obtained during the second Temple, that the phrase means to pronounce a vow distinctly, as the Chaldee versions render it, so that no vow mentally conceived was binding; the form of words is nowhere given in Scripture but was left to the administrators of the law, who divided vows into the positive and the negative.

What such a vow meant in practice is filled in. Henry supposes a man consecrating himself or a child to the tabernacle in some inferior office, sweeping the floor, carrying out ashes or running errands. Wesley distinguishes the stricter devotions, those of the Nazarites and Levites, for whom no redemption was admitted since they served in person, from the larger sort, where men not of that tribe might through zeal devote themselves or their children in some subserviency; and he explains the estimation by the danger that too many so dedicated would burden the sanctuary. Clarke states the rule plainly, that one who has vowed a living creature and wishes to redeem it shall ransom it at the priest's estimation, the priest judging the age and qualifications of the person or beast and the circumstances of the man who vowed it; and he cites Ainsworth that a vow is a religious promise made with prayer and paid with thanksgiving. Calvin says the chapter shows at what price what has been offered is to be redeemed, supposing the vows cannot conveniently be paid.

The scale itself is then read off. Keil gives the table, fifty shekels for a man between twenty and sixty and thirty for a woman, twenty and ten between five and twenty, five and three from a month to five years, fifteen and ten above sixty, all in the shekel of the sanctuary; the price followed capacity and vigour of life, the woman as the weaker vessel being appraised at half the man's amount. Ellicott notes that the estimation begins with the male as the most important person and marks his age, the years named being the prime of life, and that he is rated not by rank but by the value of his services, the sum falling on rich and poor alike. Wesley says the same in a line, that this is the best time for strength and service and so prized highest. Gill adds that the estimation was not left to the man or the priest at pleasure, and Clarke reduces the first figure to the sterling of his own day.
4:
The lower rate for the woman is explained the same way by all of them, and always from service rather than worth. Clarke says she could be redeemed for a little more than half the man's value, for the obvious reason that a woman, if employed, could not be of so much use in the service of the sanctuary. Wesley says her price is less because she is inferior to him in strength and serviceableness. Ellicott calls her the weaker vessel whose labour is of less value, and adds two observations of another kind: that thirty shekels was the price of a slave and the sum for which Christ was sold, and that Jephthah has been thought able under this provision to redeem the daughter he unwittingly vowed, though he refers the reader forward to the law of the devoted thing.

The mention of a child of five settles who is making the vow. Ellicott argues that since a vow binding a child to pay a considerable sum would be of no force, the vows here cannot be only those a man makes about his own person; the case contemplated is a father or mother vowing a child, or another person taking on himself to pay that child's value, and the following verse makes it plainer still. Gill says the same, that no child of five is supposed to vow or to make an estimation, but a grown man who says that the estimation of this little one be upon him, and is then bound to pay the value. Ellicott gives the second-Temple formula, that the estimation of this my boy or this my girl, or of that boy or girl, be upon me. Wesley notes that children might be vowed by their parents though not by themselves, and were bound by the parents' vow, which he does not find strange given the parents' right to dispose of their children so far as it is not contrary to the mind of God. At the lower limit Gill reports the Jewish rule that one less than a month old may be vowed but not estimated, and Clarke that the firstborn, being always the Lord's property already, could not be vowed at all.

The two ends of life are then compared. Clarke observes that the boy and girl of the youngest class, being both in comparative infancy, were nearly of equal value, and that the old man and old woman, being nearly past labour, stood in about the same ratio and for the same reason. Gill puts the reason simply, that at sixty a man is almost past his labour and it is high time to leave off business. Ellicott ranks the old man next in value to the child, and notices what the others pass over, that the old woman is rated at exactly the girl's rate, so that the disproportion between the sexes is not the same in age as in youth; the authorities of the second Temple accounted for it by the adage that an old man in the house is always in the way, while an old woman is a treasure, since she manages all the household affairs.

The last provision meets the man who cannot pay. Gill takes it of one so poor that he cannot pay the value set upon him, and Wesley likewise of one not able to pay the price required. Ellicott follows the procedure: the man pleading poverty presents himself before the priest, who examines his circumstances and taxes him accordingly, the minimum during the second Temple being one shekel. He adds what was done at the other end, that the goods of a man who neglected his vows were seized by the treasury officials, but so as not to deprive him of his means of subsistence, the bailiffs being obliged to leave a mechanic two sets of tools.
9:
Gill defines the first class as creatures used in sacrifice, bullocks, sheep, goats, rams and lambs, and Ellicott as the sacrificial quadrupeds. On what holy means here Ellicott is precise: such a beast could not be redeemed at all but was delivered to the sanctuary, where the priests sold it to Israelites who required sacrifices, the money maintaining the service. Wesley allows more latitude, that it was consecrated either to be sacrificed or to be given to the priest, according to the manner of the vow and the intention of him who vowed. Keil states rule and penalty together, that everything so given was to be holy and not exchanged, a good animal for a bad or a bad for a good, and that if the exchange were made both animals became holy.

The two verbs of the prohibition are weighed. Gill reports that some think them the same word twice, but that Abarbinel distinguishes them, the first an exchange across kinds, as one of the herd for one of the flock, the second within a kind. Wesley takes them as one thing said more emphatically, and gives two reasons for the strictness, that God would preserve the reverence of consecrated things, and that men might otherwise exchange under this pretence for the worse; the forfeiting of both animals he calls a just penalty for levity in weighty matters. Ellicott says the identical animal must be delivered and no change permitted, not even of a better for an inferior, the stress being marked by two verbs of the same import. Clarke states the principle, that whatever was consecrated by a vow or purpose of heart was from that moment the Lord's property, so that to change it was impiety and to withhold it sacrilege; and he turns from the law to the reader, asking whether he has paid his own vows, and whether he was not himself vowed and consecrated to God in his baptism.

The unclean beast raises a difficulty. Ellicott takes it of an animal outside the three sacrificial kinds and so incapable of being offered, but reports that the authorities of the second Temple understood the phrase of blemished oxen and sheep and goats, unlawful for the altar. Gill gives both readings, that any creature is meant except a dog, whose price was not to be brought into the house of the Lord, though some, and Jarchi among them, understand it of blemished beasts. Keil instances an ass, and says such a beast was set before the priest to be valued between good and bad, neither very high nor very low, but at a medium price. Calvin raises the question the others pass over, how it could be allowable to vow what God had forbidden to be offered and prohibited from the temple as unclean, since if any man had thought to sacrifice an unclean animal the superstition would have been rejected and expiation needed.

The valuation and the surcharge close the section. Gill says the priest was to price the beast according to its worth as it appeared to him, and Ellicott that he estimated by the condition of the animal, whatever it might be. Ellicott adds a distinction the text leaves implicit, that the estimate was meant for anyone who wished to purchase, the man who vowed it not excluded, but that the former owner alone paid a fifth above the price, probably as a fine for taking back what he had promised. Keil calls the fifth a kind of compensation for taking back the animal vowed. Clarke thinks it meant to prevent rash vows and covetous redemptions, and works the sum: valued at forty shekels, the thing cost its former owner forty-eight.
14:
Wesley notes first that the sanctifying meant is by a vow, since it is that manner the whole chapter speaks of. What became of the house is put in almost the same words by most of them. Gill says it was set apart for sacred service so that it might be sold and the money laid out in sacrifices and the repairs of the temple. Ellicott says it had to be sold and the money used for the maintenance and repair of the sanctuary, unless the house were wanted as a dwelling for the priests, and that the sale could follow only after the priest had examined and fixed its value. Henry says the money got by the sale went to the use of the sanctuary, which by degrees came to be greatly enriched with dedicated things. Keil says the same and names an opinion he rejects, Knobel's supposition that the man who vowed was to pay the valuation price if he did not redeem, which he calls quite groundless, since the unredeemed house was simply sold for the sanctuary's good. Clarke alone takes it otherwise, that it was the yearly rent of the house, once consecrated, which went towards the repairs of the tabernacle.

How far the vow reached is filled in from later practice. Ellicott reports that the second-Temple authorities took the word house to cover not only the building but anything belonging to it or any article of furniture in it, which the owner might vow separately, and that from the words his house they concluded the property must be absolutely his own. Gill supplies the rules guarding other people's claims: a wife could not demand her dowry out of what had been sanctified, nor a creditor his debt, but the man might redeem on condition of paying both, and he had no power over his wife's or his children's clothes. Calvin describes the men who made such vows, those who sought of God that they and their families might inhabit their houses in health and safety, and those who, wishing fertility for their fields, vowed some acres of them. He grants that superstitious prayers were sometimes mixed with this exercise of piety, as though favour could be bought by a bargain with God, but says that since the thing was not wrong in itself God bore indulgently with errors not easily corrected, lest in hating them he abolish what was laudable.

The redemption follows the rule already given for beasts. Gill says the house might be redeemed either by another paying the priest's price or by the original owner paying a fifth more, alike in walled cities and villages; he cites Maimonides for what followed, that a redeemed house in a walled city became absolutely the redeemer's after twelve months, while one in the villages returned to its owner at the jubilee. Ellicott notes that in the second Temple the right of redeeming at the added fifth was extended to the man's son, wife or nearest of kin, the reason being the same as with the animals. Wesley adds that the fifth could be borne the better because the priests usually put a moderate rate upon the thing. Henry gives the sharpest reason for the surcharge: the owner must not have his house as cheap as another, for he should have considered before he vowed; to the necessitous God would abate the estimation, but to the man who was fickle and humoursome, whose second thoughts inclined more to the world than his first, God would rise in the price. Henry closes by turning it to use, that there is a way of sanctifying our houses to be holy unto the Lord without either selling them or buying them back.
16:
All of them notice that only part of a field may be vowed, and that the limiting words are supplied rather than written. Clarke says they are not in the text but are generally allowed to belong there, since a man might not vow his whole estate and so make his family beggars to enrich the sanctuary, which God would not permit. Ellicott says the same and adds that the words are implied in the Hebrew construction. Gill gives two reasons, that the man might keep something to live on for his family, and that estates might not be alienated altogether from the families and tribes they belonged to. Wesley adds a third, that by vowing away all his possessions a man disabled himself from divers duties and became burdensome to his brethren. Gill and Ellicott both note that the field is one held by inheritance, distinguished from a field of the man's own purchase.

The valuation is reckoned not by acres but by seed. Keil explains that the price followed the measure of seed sown, an omer of barley being appraised at fifty shekels, and he works out the size of the measure from the ephah and from the calculation of Thenius. Wesley says it more plainly, that the estimate went by the quantity and quality of the land, known by the seed it can receive and return. Clarke reports the rabbinic rule that the land, good or bad, was valued at forty-eight shekels for all the years of the jubilee, if it were large enough to sow a homer of barley.

The price then moves with the calendar. Ellicott says the fifty shekels apply only where the vow is made immediately after a jubilee year, the period covered being forty-nine years; if the vow falls later, the priest values by the years remaining to the next jubilee, the elapsed years being deducted and so many shekels taken off. Keil gives the same rule, that where the vow follows the jubilee immediately no alteration is made, and otherwise the price is abated. Gill takes the first case of the jubilee year itself, current or just past, citing Aben Ezra, and Jarchi for the case where a purchaser comes forward as soon as the field is valued. Wesley states the result in a line, that the defalcation is more or less as the years are more or fewer.

The last verses deal with a man who will not redeem. Ellicott observes that the low value fixed per acre was designed so that the field should be redeemed by him, and that the second-Temple rule extended the right to his wife and heirs; if he foregoes the privilege he shows no desire to perpetuate his family name, and if he then sells the vowed field to another he adds fraud to it. Wesley reads the sequence as the priest offering it to him first and, on his refusal, selling it, after which he for ever loses the benefit of redemption. Gill puts it more mildly, that he will not give the settled price with the fifth besides, and chooses rather that it be used for what he devoted it to. Clarke says the field is then under the ban, so devoted to God as never more to be capable of redemption, and Ellicott that when it leaves the purchaser's hand at the jubilee it does not revert to the man who vowed it but becomes God's property. Keil and Wesley add that the possession falls to the priest; and Wesley answers the objection that this conflicts with the law giving the priests no inheritance, since that was spoken of the tribe in general with reference to the first division of the land.
22:
The case now changes, and they are careful to say why. Gill describes the field as one bought with the man's own money from someone in poverty and distress who was obliged to sell it, and which by the earlier law returned to its original proprietor in the year of jubilee. Ellicott says the case is necessarily different for that reason, since such a field is the buyer's only until the next jubilee, when it reverts to the hereditary owner; a leased field of that kind, when vowed, has to be dealt with by another rule than the one just given. Wesley marks the same distinction from the other side, glossing the possession of the preceding verses as a man's patrimony or inheritance.

What that other rule is Ellicott states most fully. The man who vows a purchased field does not pay the low rate fixed for a family inheritance; the priest values it in proportion to the number of crops it will yield up to the jubilee, in the same way as fields are valued in ordinary purchases. Two consequences follow. The valuation had to be paid at once, and it was paid without the additional fifth part which fell on the redemption of an hereditary field; whereas the man who vowed an hereditary field had the advantage of paying the smaller sum in yearly instalments. Gill puts the reckoning plainly, that the priest was to estimate the purchased field and set a price on it according to the best of his judgment, and give it to the man who sanctified it or to whoever would redeem it, the price being made according to the number of years remaining until the jubilee. Wesley reads the estimation as the price Moses had been directed to set in such cases, and the term as covering only the space between the making of the vow and the jubilee, since the man had no right to the field for any longer time; the sum paid he calls a holy thing, as being consecrated to God in place of the land redeemed by it. Keil notes only that the estimation was to be given in that day as a holy thing to the Lord.

Where the field goes at the jubilee is then settled, and Gill is careful to exclude two claimants who might have been expected. It returns neither to the man who sanctified it, whether he redeemed it or not, nor to anyone who bought it from the treasurer of the temple after it had been sanctified, but to the original proprietor and owner from whom the man who vowed it had bought it in the first place. Ellicott says the same and refers it to the standing law of the jubilee, that the field thus vowed did not return to the purchaser but to the hereditary owner.

The chapter then fixes the coin in which all these sums are reckoned. Clarke calls it a standard shekel, the standard being kept in the sanctuary in order to try and regulate all the weights in the land by it. Gill guards the phrase against a misunderstanding: it does not mean that there was a shekel in the sanctuary different from the common one, since every shekel ought to have been like that one, of the full weight and worth of it; the point is that both the estimation and the payment were to be in money of full weight. Ellicott gives the reason for insisting on it, that since the proceeds of these vows were devoted to the maintenance and repair of the sanctuary, the valuations were to be made and paid by the standard weight of the sanctuary shekel. Keil states the rule in a line, that all valuations were to be made according to that shekel.
26:
The firstling is excepted, and the reason is the same in every hand. Keil states it as a rule, that what belonged to the Lord by law could not be dedicated to him by a vow. Calvin gives the motive it guards against: since men are greatly given to ostentation, God forbids the firstborn to be offered him, since that would be to present stolen goods, and they are not by consecrating what is already his to steal from him in their fictitious liberality; nor should we be surprised, the ambition to lay God under obligation being almost natural to us all. Wesley says it more sharply, that to vow such a thing is a tacit derogation from the Lord's right and a mocking of God by pretending to give what we cannot withhold. Henry calls it making a jest of sanctifying things to the Lord, and distinguishes: though a general vow may cover what we were already bound to, as in our sacramental covenant, a singular vow should be of what we were not antecedently bound to. Ellicott prefers the rendering nevertheless, and observes that the legislator, having ruled on the four classes that may be vowed, closes by naming two exceptions.

The unclean firstling is caught between two disqualifications. Wesley puts them plainly, that it could not be vowed because it was a firstborn nor offered because it was unclean, and is therefore to be redeemed or sold. Gill narrows the case, that this is not the firstling of unclean creatures in general, redeemed with a lamb, but such as were vowed for the reparation of the sanctuary, citing Jarchi. Ellicott and Keil both notice that the rule stands at variance with the earlier law, by which an ass was either redeemed with a sheep or put to death.

With the ban a different kind of vow begins. Gill marks the difference: sanctifying and devoting were both vows, but the latter had an execration added, by which a man imprecated a curse on himself if what he devoted were put to any other use, so that the vow was absolute and irrevocable and what was vowed unalienable. Clarke says it in a line, that the ban always meant an absolute unredeemable grant to God. Wesley explains most holy as meaning that the thing might be handled by the priests only, not even by their own families. Ellicott measures how far the power reached, since a man might ban not only his cattle and his inalienable inherited land but the human beings over whom he had control, his children and his slaves. Henry marks the distinction between things devoted and things merely sanctified as the point of the passage.

The last verse is the hardest, and they close ranks around it. Gill argues from the wording that it cannot mean men devoted to the Lord as in the verse before, since the phrase unto the Lord is absent, but men devoted to ruin, for whom there is no redemption; and that the text says devoted of men, from among men, not by men. Wesley presses the same point, that men here are not the persons devoting but those devoted to destruction, whether by God's own sentence or by men in pursuance of it, and warns that no man might by this text devote his own child. Clarke reports that the law has been appealed to by the enemies of divine revelation as proof that human sacrifices were offered under Moses, and refuses the inference: had there been such a law it would have been explicitly revealed and not left in a few obscure words; some take the devoted person to become the Lord's property or to serve him till death. Ellicott allows the plain sense of putting to death but denies the sacrificial construction, the man being not offered to God but removed out of his sight.
30:
The tithe is the second thing that cannot be vowed, and for the same reason. Ellicott says expressly that, like the firstborn of animals, the tithes already belong to God by another statute, so that a man cannot vow what is not his own. Clarke says God claims it as his own, a point perfectly settled and free of difficulty. Calvin takes it further back: in assigning the tithes to the Levites God ceded his own rights, since they were a kind of royal revenue, and so bars all complaint; the priests are his receivers, collecting in his name what could not be refused without sacrilegious fraud. Gill distinguishes the several sorts, the first tithe, the tithe out of the tithe, the second and the poor's; Wesley narrows the reference to the ordinary yearly tithes of the Levites, as the provision for redemption implies.

Ellicott notes the same asymmetry as in the earlier laws: a man may not vow his tithes, but may redeem them by adding a fifth, while by the rule of the second Temple anyone might redeem another man's tithes at the exact value without the fifth, the money being carried to Jerusalem. Gill gives the same from Jarchi, that the fifth was added for a man's own tithes and not his neighbour's, and Calvin that it was not for the Levites' profit. Keil records the rule for the flocks, that no discrimination was to be made between good and bad and no exchange, and that if one were made both became holy.

The manner of tithing cattle is described from the Jewish authorities, Clarke and Ellicott giving the same scene in nearly the same words. The flock was shut into one fold with a door so narrow that two could not pass together; the dams stood outside; as they bleated the young ran out to meet them, while the owner stood at the door with a rod dipped in vermilion, marking every tenth. Ellicott adds the canonists' rule that the beast must pass of itself and not be brought out. Wesley leaves the choice open between the tither's rod, since the Jews drove their cattle through a narrow passage where the tenth was marked for the priest, and the shepherd's rod, under which the herds passed and were numbered. Gill notes from the Targums that the law concerns oxen and sheep only, none but clean beasts being tithed.

The prohibition on searching follows from the method. Gill says the owner was not to consider whether the beast was fat or lean, perfect or blemished, but to take it as it was, and Ellicott that he was to mark every tenth as it left the fold. The closing verse Gill refers either to this chapter or rather to the whole book, placing the giving of it near Sinai; Ellicott glosses the mountain as the mountainous district. Clarke thinks the conclusion very like the one ending the previous chapter, and repeats his supposition that this chapter should have followed the twenty-fifth, the twenty-sixth having originally ended the book. Calvin says the passage commends the Law promulgated on the two tables with the declarations annexed to explain the mind of God, and that Moses seeks belief for it from its authority, as delivered by God, and from his own calling, having not assumed the office of lawgiver but been appointed to it. Henry and Wesley close alike, that many of these precepts are moral and always binding while others are ceremonial and peculiar to that economy, yet instructive to us who have the key to their mysteries; and that we have cause to bless God that we are not under the dark shadows of the law, the doctrine of reconciliation by a Mediator being no longer clouded with the smoke of burning sacrifice but cleared by the knowledge of Christ and him crucified.
